Accounts

The accounts app: the custom user model, registration, and the role groups and their permissions.

accounts.models

The accounts app’s model: the custom user, with a role and subscriptions.

class accounts.models.User(*args, **kwargs)[source]

A user of the news application, with one of four roles: reader, journalist, editor, or publisher.

The role decides the user’s group, and the group decides their permissions. Readers can also subscribe to publications and to journalists.

Variables:

  • ROLE_CHOICES – The four roles, READER, JOURNALIST, EDITOR, and PUBLISHER, each with the name shown for it.

  • ROLE_GROUPS – The group for each role. The groups, and the permissions they grant, must be created during database setup for users to be saved.

  • email – The user’s email address. Required and unique, because password reset links are sent by email and approved articles are emailed to subscribers.

  • role – The user’s role. Each user has exactly one, chosen at registration, and it never changes.

  • subscribed_publications – Readers only. The publications the reader subscribes to, covering all of each publication’s articles.

  • subscribed_journalists – Readers only, and only journalists can be subscribed to. The journalists the reader subscribes to, covering just each journalist’s independent articles, not those they write for a publication.

save(*args, **kwargs)[source]

Save the user, and place them in their role’s group and no other.

Parameters:

  • args – Passed on to Django’s Model.save().

  • kwargs – Passed on to Django’s Model.save().

Raises:

ImproperlyConfigured – If the role’s group does not exist, because the groups have not been set up yet.

accounts.forms

The accounts app’s form: registration, with an email address and a role.

class accounts.forms.RegistrationForm(*args, **kwargs)[source]

Form to register a new User account.

Built on Django’s UserCreationForm, which provides the username field, the two password fields, and these checks:

  • the username is not already in use.

  • the two passwords match.

  • the password passes Django’s password validators.

This form limits usernames to 20 letters and digits, and adds the email and role fields from the User model. The model makes email required and unique, and limits role to the roles in User.ROLE_CHOICES, so the form checks both.

Variables:

username – The username field. It replaces the one the form would otherwise build from the model, which allows up to 150 characters, including @ . + - and _. Here a username is at most 20 characters, using only the letters A to Z (upper or lower case) and the digits 0 to 9.

property media

Return all media required to render the widgets on this form.

Management commands

The setup_groups_and_permissions management command, which creates the four role groups and gives each one its permissions.

Django management commands

A management command is a task you run from the command line through manage.py, such as migrate, runserver, or createsuperuser. A project can add its own commands, and this file is one of them.

How Django finds a command

Django looks in the management/commands/ folder of every app in INSTALLED_APPS. Both management/ and management/commands/ need an __init__.py file. Each other .py file in management/commands/ becomes a command named after the file. For example, this file:

accounts/management/commands/setup_groups_and_permissions.py

becomes:

python manage.py setup_groups_and_permissions

How a command works

The file must contain a class named exactly Command, built on Django’s BaseCommand. When the command runs, Django calls the class’s handle() method, which is where the work is done. The class can also have:

  • help: the description shown by python manage.py help <command>.

  • add_arguments(): for options, such as --dry-run.

Inside handle(), self.stdout.write() prints output, and raising CommandError stops the command with an error message.

How to run a command

From the folder that contains manage.py:

python manage.py <command>

To list every available command, including the project’s own:

python manage.py help

To show one command’s description and options:

python manage.py help <command>
accounts.management.commands.setup_groups_and_permissions.GROUP_PERMISSIONS = {'editor': ['view_article', 'change_article', 'delete_article', 'approve_article', 'view_newsletter', 'change_newsletter', 'delete_newsletter', 'view_publication'], 'journalist': ['add_article', 'view_article', 'change_article', 'delete_article', 'approve_article', 'add_newsletter', 'view_newsletter', 'change_newsletter', 'delete_newsletter', 'view_publication'], 'publisher': ['view_article', 'view_newsletter', 'add_publication', 'view_publication', 'change_publication', 'delete_publication'], 'reader': ['view_article', 'view_newsletter', 'view_publication']}

The permissions each role’s group gets, as Django permission codenames (action_model). Every model here is in the news app. For example:

"add_article"       # may create articles
"view_publication"  # may view publications

Most are the four permissions Django creates for every model: add, view, change, and delete. approve_article is a custom permission, declared in the Article model’s Meta class. It says only that a role may approve articles at all; news/access.py decides which articles.

class accounts.management.commands.setup_groups_and_permissions.Command(stdout=None, stderr=None, no_color=False, force_color=False)[source]

Create the four role groups and give each group its permissions.

Run it after the tables are built with migrate_all, and again after remove_groups_and_permissions:

python manage.py setup_groups_and_permissions

It is safe to run again. Groups that already exist are kept, and each group’s permissions are replaced with exactly its list in GROUP_PERMISSIONS, so the groups always match it.

handle(*args, **options)[source]

Create or update each group, then set its permissions.

Parameters:

  • args – Positional arguments from Django. Not used.

  • options – The command’s options, from Django. Not used.

Raises:

CommandError – If a permission does not exist yet, which means the migrations have not been run, or a custom permission is not declared.

The remove_groups_and_permissions management command.

Deletes the four role groups that setup_groups_and_permissions creates, which undoes it. Deleting a group also removes its permissions and every user’s membership in it. The permissions themselves are kept, because Django creates them from the models, and the user accounts are kept too.

Until the groups are set up again, no user can be saved, because User.save() needs their role’s group to exist.

How to run it

From the folder that contains manage.py:

python manage.py remove_groups_and_permissions

It asks you to type yes before deleting anything. To skip the question:

python manage.py remove_groups_and_permissions --no-input

To create the groups again afterward:

python manage.py setup_groups_and_permissions

It only runs while DEBUG is True, so it cannot change a live site.

class accounts.management.commands.remove_groups_and_permissions.Command(stdout=None, stderr=None, no_color=False, force_color=False)[source]

Delete the Readers, Publishers, Editors, and Journalists groups.

Run it with:

python manage.py remove_groups_and_permissions

Other groups, permissions, and user accounts are not touched.

add_arguments(parser)[source]

Add the --no-input option, which skips the yes question.

Parameters:

parser – The command’s argument parser, from Django.

handle(*args, **options)[source]

Ask for confirmation, then delete the role groups.

Parameters:

  • args – Positional arguments from Django. Not used.

  • options – The command’s options, from Django. The interactive option is False when --no-input is given.

Raises:

CommandError – If DEBUG is False, or the answer is not yes.
